To perspire means to release sweat through the skin. Your body has millions of tiny openings in your skin called pores. When your body needs to cool itself down — or when you feel strong emotions like fear or nervousness — it pushes a salty liquid out through these pores. That process is called perspiring.

The liquid your body releases is called perspiration (the noun form of this verb), which is just another word for sweat.

Your body perspires for a few main reasons:

  • Heat — When it's hot outside, or you're in a warm room, your body perspires to bring your temperature down. As the moisture evaporates from your skin, it cools you off. Think of it as your body's built-in air conditioning.
  • Physical effort — When you exercise, run, or do heavy physical work, your muscles generate heat. Your body perspires to release that heat.
  • Strong emotions — Nervousness, fear, anxiety, or excitement can all make you perspire. You've probably felt this before an important exam or a stressful moment — your palms get damp, your forehead feels moist. That's perspiring.
  • Illness — When you have a fever, your body often perspires as it tries to fight off the sickness and regulate its temperature.
  • Spicy food — Eating very spicy food can also trigger perspiring, especially on the face and scalp.

Both words describe exactly the same bodily process. However, they differ in tone and social register:

  • Sweat is the everyday, casual word. Most people use it in normal conversation: "I was sweating like crazy at the gym."
  • Perspire is the formal and polite version. It is preferred in professional, medical, or refined social contexts: "The patient began to perspire during the examination."

In fact, there is a well-known old saying in English: "Horses sweat, men perspire, and ladies merely glow." This saying humorously captures the idea that "perspire" was historically considered the more dignified word, while "sweat" was seen as too blunt or crude for polite company. Today, this distinction is softer — both words are perfectly acceptable — but "perspire" still carries a more formal, clinical, or refined feel.

In medical textbooks, doctor's notes, and formal writing, you will almost always see "perspire" or "perspiration" rather than "sweat."

Since you're a learner, here are all the forms you'll encounter:

  • perspire — base form: "I perspire a lot in summer."
  • perspires — third person singular (he/she/it): "She perspires when she's anxious."
  • perspired — past tense and past participle: "He perspired throughout the interview."
  • perspiring — present participle (ongoing action): "She was perspiring heavily after the run."
  • perspiration — the noun (the sweat itself, or the act): "Beads of perspiration formed on his forehead."
Common Collocations (Words That Often Go with "Perspire")

Certain words pair naturally with "perspire" in English:

  • perspire heavily / profusely — to perspire a lot: "He perspired profusely in the August heat."
  • perspire freely — to perspire without restraint, often used in a positive medical sense: "The body is designed to perspire freely during exercise."
  • begin to perspire / start to perspire — to start the process: "She began to perspire as soon as she stepped onto the stage."
  • perspire with effort / nervousness / heat — to name the cause: "He perspired with the effort of carrying the boxes up three flights of stairs."

Here are sentences that show the word used naturally, so you can see how it fits into real language:

  1. "The runners perspired heavily in the midday sun."
  2. "He noticed he was perspiring when the interviewer asked him a difficult question."
  3. "A healthy body perspires to regulate its temperature."
  4. "She stepped out of the sauna, perspiring and relaxed."
  5. "The doctor noted that the patient had begun to perspire, which was a sign the fever was breaking."
  6. "Even sitting still in the crowded room, people were perspiring."

Sometimes "perspire" is used slightly humorously or self-consciously — precisely because it sounds so formal. If someone says "I'm perspiring a little" instead of "I'm sweating buckets," they might be making a gentle joke, trying to sound refined in an undignified situation. This kind of playful use of formal vocabulary is common in English, so if you ever see "perspire" used with a light, ironic tone, that's why.

Perspire means to release sweat through the pores of your skin. It happens due to heat, exercise, emotions, illness, or spicy food. It is the formal and polite synonym for sweat, commonly found in medical, professional, and careful writing. The related noun is perspiration. You can perspire heavily, profusely, or freely, and you perspire with heat, effort, or nervousness.
